title: State Sen. Glen Meyer votes for LB965, broadening sexual abuse laws and protections
text:
State Sen. Glen Meyer votes for LB965, broadening sexual abuse laws and protections
State Sen. Glen Meyer of District 17 voted yes on LB965, which expands sexual offense laws and protections for certain vulnerable groups, on April 10, 2026, during the 109th Legislature. The floor vote was recorded as a roll call and listed as "Passed on Final Reading" with the Legislature's tally of ayes to noes to senators not voting at 39-10-0, according to the Nebraska Unicameral Legislature.
The Nebraska Legislature officially describes the measure as "Prohibit sexual abuse of a probationer or problem solving court participant and sexual abuse by a conservator, guardian, guardian ad litem, or child welfare service provider; change provisions relating to protection orders, certain offenses, attorney's fees, and victim notification requirements; and provide requirements for immunity for probation employees, Brady-Giglio disclosures, confidentiality for certain officers, registration under the Sex Offender Registration Act, county conflict counsel, and determinations of the best interest of the child".
Below is our breakdown, based on the linked official bill material; it may include interpretive clarifications of its provisions.
The bill expands Nebraska sexual-offense statutes to cover sexual abuse of probationers, participants in problem-solving courts, people served by conservators, guardians or guardians ad litem, and minors in the care of child welfare service providers, making such conduct first- or second-degree felonies and barring consent as a defense. It broadens incest to include sexual contact or penetration with adopted and foster children, adds those offenses to child protection, victim notification, evidence and confidentiality statutes, and requires those convicted to register under the Sex Offender Registration Act. The bill also grants civil and criminal immunity to probation employees who administer opioid overdose reversal medication in good faith.
Glen Meyer was elected to the Nebraska Legislature in 2024 to represent District 17. He graduated from Pender High School and has held leadership roles in local organizations, including service on the Thurston County Board of Supervisors and the Northeast Nebraska Public Health Board.
Bill details in this report reflect the public legislative record at the time of publication.
In Nebraska, the legislative process begins when a senator files a bill in the state's single-chamber Legislature. Most bills go to a standing committee and receive a public hearing. If advanced, a bill moves through General File and Select File, where senators may debate and amend it, before reaching Final Reading for a vote. After final passage, the bill is sent to the governor, who has five days, excluding Sundays, to sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature.
The Nebraska Legislature convenes annually on the first Wednesday after the first Monday in January, with 90 working days in odd-numbered years and 60 working days in even-numbered years.
